title: What will be the US national debt on December 31, 2026?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the "Total Public Debt Outstanding" on December 31, 2026, according to the official [Debt to the Penny dataset](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/debt-to-the-penny/debt-to-the-penny).
background:
The [national debt of the United States](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/debt-to-the-penny/debt-to-the-penny#introduction) is the debt, or unpaid borrowed funds, carried by the federal government of the United States, which is measured by intra-governmental holdings and debt held by the public, including securities issued by the U.S. Treasury. The U.S. national debt has been [climbing at a rapid pace](https://www.foxbusiness.com/economy/us-national-debt-tracker) for years.

At the end of 2025, [the national debt](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/debt-to-the-penny/debt-to-the-penny#introduction) stood at just over \$38.5 trillion. By mid-August 2026, the figure had reached [over \$40 trillion](https://apnews.com/article/treasury-national-debt-limit-a27a8d3651ff810b25c610d3e1b6259d), equivalent to about a 4% increase, and over \$6 billion per day during 2026.

comments.author: DeRuina
comments.text:
One thing I'd flag for anyone anchoring on Treasury's borrowing estimate: the August 3 refunding statement projected \$628B of privately-held net marketable borrowing for Oct–Dec 2026, but that number excludes intergovernmental holdings, and this question resolves on total public debt outstanding. In each of the last three years, Q4 intergovernmental debt rose by roughly \$220–310B, with a chunk of it landing on December 31 itself when semiannual interest is credited to the trust funds. So the marketable estimate is closer to a floor than a central figure for the Sep 30 to Dec 31 change, which has run \$750–880B in 2023–2025 (Debt to the Penny). The cash drawdown from \$950B to \$850B cuts the other way, but only partially.



The other constraint is the \$41.1T debt limit. Total debt outstanding runs only about \$30B above the "subject to limit" figure, so unless Congress raises the ceiling in the lame-duck session, the December 31 total can't materially exceed \~\$41.13T. If borrowing runs hot, the likelier outcome is a number pinned just under the limit rather than one well above it, which is why I have very little mass above 41.2T.



Watch the November refunding statement for whether it revises the Q4 borrowing estimate upward again, as happened repeatedly this year.

comments.author: DaiLothbrook
comments.text: The strongest evidence here is the Treasury’s expectation of \$628 billion in net marketable borrowing during the final quarter of 2026. Mapping that estimate to total-debt growth using the two most recent comparable years produces a year-end center near \$41.13 trillion. Because this is a direct forecast for the relevant quarter, I give it more weight than a broad seasonal average and substantially narrow the distribution. I place the lower quartile at \$41.04 trillion, the median at \$41.13 trillion and the upper quartile at \$41.22 trillion. My main reservation is that the conversion rests on only two calibration years.

comments.author: Koboh
comments.text:
That estimate is more defensible than simply extending an annual CBO debt to GDP forecast because Treasury’s actual daily debt data and its latest borrowing plans give us a much more direct way to estimate the December 31 level.

**My Estimate:**

| Item                               | Approx. figure         |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| Gross federal debt, Sept. 25, 2026 | \$40.069T              |
| Days from Sept. 25 to Dec. 31      | 97                     |
| Recent average daily increase      | roughly \$7–8B/day     |
| Implied increase to Dec. 31        | roughly \$0.68–\$0.78T |
| Estimated Dec. 31, 2026 debt       | \$40.75–\$40.85T       |
| My central estimate                | ≈ \$40.8T              |
| Plausible wider range              | \$40.5–\$41.1T         |

Treasury’s debt to the penny data put gross federal debt at approximately **\$40.069 trillion on September 25**.

![](https://cdn.metaculus.com/user_uploaded/image_B6dMGAK.jpeg)

[https://www.foxbusiness.com/economy/us-national-debt-tracker](https://www.foxbusiness.com/economy/us-national-debt-tracker)

**I would put the estimate near \$40.8T**

The important thing is to separate the annual deficit from the national debt.

CBO’s February 2026 baseline projected a **\$1.9 trillion FY2026 deficit**, with debt held by the public at about 101% of GDP. But that is a fiscal-year measure ending September 30, not a December 31 debt forecast. CBO also explains that changes in cash balances and other financing activities can make the change in debt different from the budget deficit. 

![](https://cdn.metaculus.com/user_uploaded/image_JvY8krP.jpeg)

[https://www.cbo.gov/publication/62105](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/62105)

<u>*A simple scenario table*</u>

| Scenario                         | Average increase from Sept. 25 | Dec. 31 estimate |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------- |
| Slower accumulation              | \$5B/day                       | \$40.55T         |
| Moderate                         | \$6B/day                       | \$40.65T         |
| Recent-trend case                | \$7.35B/day                    | \$40.78T         |
| Faster                           | \$8B/day                       | \$40.84T         |
| Very high                        | \$9B/day                       | \$40.94T         |
| Extremely high / financing-heavy | \$10B/day                      | \$41.04T         |

<u>***My final call***</u>

If I had to put **one number** on December 31, 2026:

**U.S. gross national debt: approximately \$40.8 trillion**

I’d use **\$40.8T as the point estimate**, with **\$40.5T–\$41.1T** as a reasonable uncertainty range.

“The interesting part is that **\$41 trillion is no longer a distant milestone**. The debt crossed \$40 trillion in 2026, and the Treasury’s own borrowing plans plus the recent daily trajectory put another roughly \$0.7–\$0.9 trillion within reach before the end of the year.”

1. Privately-held net marketable borrowing excludes rollovers (auction “add-ons”) of Treasury securities held in the SOMA but includes financing required due to SOMA redemptions.  Secondary market purchases of Treasury securities by SOMA do not directly change privately-held net marketable borrowing but, all else equal, when the securities mature and assuming the Federal Reserve does not redeem any maturing securities, would increase the amount of cash raised for a given privately-held auction size by increasing the SOMA “add-on” amount.  Additionally, buybacks are not expected to significantly affect privately-held net marketable borrowing as new issuance replaces securities that are bought back.

comments.author: lubossaloky
comments.text: I have updated slightly higher, to move closer to the community forecast. This question is quite complex, with multiple key factors, and requires diverse views. I think the community forecast should be trusted.

comments.author: Russell-viper
comments.text: @(Theomachado) Thanks you for pointing it out.

comments.author: lubossaloky
comments.text:
@(Theomachado) Thanks for the comprehensive analysis, including second-order catalysts, looks good! I admit that my forecast is quite shallow and only approximate. I have increased a simple linear trend a bit, but it seems your analysis suggests moving even higher.

Your analysis uses the last three years to establish a base rate, but I would suggest focusing heavily on the last completed fiscal year (FY2025), even though it includes about four months of the previous administration. FY2023 and FY2024 fall under the previous administration and have relatively lower utility for establishing the base rate.

This question closes on December 1, so I have some time to adjust. I hope I won't forget to review this question once per week.

comments.author: Theomachado
comments.text:
@(Russell-viper)

Hey @(Russell-viper), really nice forecasting, and I agree with most of the drivers. However, your stated limit of 41.1T missed the (unamortized discount + FFB), so total debt can print up to \$41.3T before the ceiling binds. On top of that, more is already committed for future expenditure than your trend is capturing, mainly due to the 628B disclosed by the Treasury, as you can see here: [https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0584](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0584). I lay out the full build-up and the waterfall in my comment above. I would appreciate your feedback to see whether I am missing any of your points, and I'm curious whether the committed borrowing plus the wall at \$41.3T (not \$41.1T) changes your mind, or whether I'm missing something on your side.
